key_insight: Patient-level splits prevent subject leakage but cannot rule out diagnostic predictions driven by acquisition-related confounders shared across folds.
clinical_relevance: High benchmark accuracy alone may not establish that a medical imaging model detects pathology rather than differences in how patients were recruited or scanned.
method: Audit whether a candidate confounder predicts diagnosis and can be decoded from images.
Test whether model scores depend on the confounder and whether images add predictive value beyond it.
Measure discrimination after controlling for the confounder.
evidence_signal: Across 236 DMR-IR patients with patient-disjoint evaluation, acquisition date predicted malignancy at AUROC 0.980 versus 0.949 for the best imaging arm; no imaging arm improved on date alone in paired folds.
watch_item: Only eight cross-label same-date pairs from ten patients were available, limiting reliable evaluation within acquisition-date groups and attribution of residual performance to pathology.
paper_title: Leakage-Free Is Not Confounder-Free: What a Patient-Level Split Cannot Certify About a Medical Imaging Benchmark
